Zig.reasoning: 5 of 7 satisfied -> 'Adequate' (exactly 5). Not 80: P6a and P6b both fail on positive evidence. Not 40: P1-P5 are each positively evidenced, including one of the strongest cross-target results in the set - a foreign-OS, foreign-architecture ELF binary built with no additional toolchain installation. Zig's low Portability level relative to C++ and Java is caused entirely by language-definition independence (P6a, P6b), not by platform reach.

cross_language_consistency_note: One indicator set (P1, P2, P3, P4, P5, P6a, P6b) was applied mechanically to all ten languages and the level was read off the satisfied count with no holistic step, per global_rules.indicator_model. Evidence was collected in the frozen global_rules.evidence_collection_order (Python, C++, Rust, Go, Java, TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift, Zig, Quidra LAST); no threshold or interpretation was settled after seeing Quidra. Four uniform tests fixed what each level means. (1) P1/P2 were scored from a single class of artifact for every language: the current official release's downloadable toolchain assets, enumerated from the project's own release API or download manifest, counting distinct OS families and distinct CPU architecture families. (2) P3 used the frozen per-language port1_cross_target command verbatim, with the frozen _general_rules.virtual_machine_targets_and_P3 rule applied identically to Java, Kotlin and TypeScript (artifact produced on host AND an official sentence that it runs on another OS/CPU family without rebuilding). Exit status, produced path and a file-type identification were recorded for every native language. (3) P6a used one mechanical test for all ten: does a first-party document designate itself normative AND state conformance, OR does a standards body independent of the implementation publish the language? Each candidate specification's full extracted text was scanned for 'normative' and 'conform*' and the hit counts recorded. Go (0/0), Kotlin (0/0), Zig (0/0), Python (0/0), Swift (explicit disclaimer), Rust (no normativity designation; the Reference declines to say whether itself or the compiler is correct) and Quidra (0/0 across every first-party document) all fail; only C++ (ISO/IEC 14882) and Java (JLS normative/non-normative split plus a conformance statement) pass. TypeScript fails because its specification is no longer published at all. (4) P5 was scored as the four-way conjunction it is written as, with no partial credit, against first-party standard-library documentation only. Nine languages document all four areas; Quidra documents three and has no filesystem path-manipulation API, which is why it loses P5 while keeping file I/O, clock and environment/process. Cross-check of the ten assignments: no two languages with the same satisfied set received different levels, and no two with different satisfied sets received the same level for different reasons - the five languages at 60 (Python, TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift, Zig) are tied at exactly 5 satisfied indicators and are reported at equal rank per global_rules.tie_handling, with no tie-break applied. Python reaches 5 by a different route than the other four (it loses P3 and P6a but keeps P6b, while they lose P6a and P6b but keep P3); the rubric counts indicators and does not weight them, so the equal level is the rubric-mandated result. No age adjustment, incumbency discount or potential-based credit was applied anywhere, in either direction.
limitations: Rust P3 (E1): the frozen recipe's cross-target build could not be completed on this host because the x86_64-apple-darwin standard library is absent from the Homebrew-repackaged rustc install and `rustup target add` is forbidden by global_rules.host_verification.no_installation_of_extra_software. Recorded as availability_state S2, verification_status unverified, NOT SATISFIED, exactly as the frozen recipe and global_rules.tool_availability_states.scoring_effect pre-registered. This is a host-provisioning and rule-interaction outcome, not a finding that Rust lacks cross-compilation; an auditor comparing Rust's 40 against Go's 80 and Zig's 60 must read this note.

Quidra P4: satisfied on a README sentence plus the machine-readable `quidra describe` field supported_platforms, both of which name three platforms and state their status as supported. Quidra publishes no tiered support table. The indicator's text requires 'an explicit platform-support list that names supported platforms and their support status' and offers a tiered table or a supported-platforms page only as examples, so a single-status list satisfies it. The same generous reading is what admits Java's prose 'Operating System Requirements' paragraph in doc/building.md, so the reading is symmetric. A stricter reading requiring differentiated tiers would drop Quidra to 2 satisfied indicators - still level 'Narrow', score 20 - so this call does not change Quidra's level.

Document-root scope: several P4/P6 citations sit on an official project's site or repository at a path outside the exact official_docs_root prefix frozen in official_project_table (Rust: forge.rust-lang.org; Go: go.dev/wiki; Java: the JLS/JVMS at docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/ and doc/building.md in openjdk/jdk; TypeScript: nodejs/node BUILDING.md and www.typescriptlang.org root; Zig: ziglang.org/download release notes; Swift: developer.apple.com/documentation/foundation). Every one is published by a member of that language's frozen official_project_set or is that language's frozen official_implementation_repository. The same latitude was extended to all ten languages including Quidra (README.md and `quidra describe`), so no language is advantaged.

Java P6b: no single Oracle or OpenJDK page names the Eclipse JDT Core compiler as a compatible implementation was found. The indicator was satisfied on the JLS preface's acknowledgement of Java language-feature implementations in javac, Eclipse and IntelliJ, together with official_project_table's frozen listing of OpenJDK and eclipse-jdt/eclipse.jdt.core as Java's two major implementations under a selection rule that itself requires official acknowledgement. A reviewer who rejects both would move Java from 100 to 80.

C++ P5: scored against the publicly retrievable WG21 working draft N4950 rather than the purchased ISO/IEC 14882 text, because the published standard is not free to retrieve. The draft is hosted by WG21, which is in C++'s frozen official_project_set.

P1/P2 for Python count the Android embeddable packages as the third OS family alongside the macOS and Windows installers. The indicator admits 'installers, archives or release assets'. Under a narrower reading that counts only development-toolchain installers, Python would have 2 OS families, lose P1, and fall to 4 satisfied indicators and level 'Partial' (40).

Swift P1/P2 were verified from swift.org's install pages (macOS, Linux with x86_64 and aarch64 signatures, Windows via WinGet); the swiftlang/swift GitHub release swift-6.4.0-RELEASE carries 0 attached assets, so the release-asset channel used for LLVM, Kotlin and Quidra was not available for Swift and the equivalent official download pages were used instead.
No E4, E5, E6 or E7 evidence is used by this metric; the frozen rubric names only E1, E2 and E3 for Portability.
